lessons.title: What you are building
lessons.why: Every later component exists to produce and improve this next-token distribution.
objectives: Explain what you are building in your own words.
Work through the numerical example and justify each step.
Produce the exercise evidence described below.
explanation: AI is the broad goal of building systems that perform tasks associated with intelligence. Machine learning fits behavior from examples; deep learning uses layered neural networks. A language model assigns probabilities to token sequences. GPT means Generative Pretrained Transformer: a model trained to continue text using a Transformer architecture. A learned program still has code, but its numerical parameters are fitted instead of being individually specified by the programmer.

Learning is a search over functions. You choose a family of functions, choose a way to score their outputs, then let an optimizer adjust the numbers inside that family. Data is evidence for those adjustments, not a list of instructions to execute. This explains both the flexibility and the failure modes: a model can find a pattern that scores well on examples while missing the rule you intended.

Our learning-scale GPT starts with random weights and a tiny corpus. Its first success is a tested forward/backward computation and better held-out prediction than a baseline. The practical assistant has a different bar: translating unseen requirements correctly. We will compare pretrained models and deterministic rules rather than expecting the small educational GPT to know the world.

lessons.title: Training, inference & model dimensions
lessons.why: Correct dimension bookkeeping prevents nearly every early GPT implementation error.
objectives: Explain training, inference & model dimensions in your own words.
Work through the numerical example and justify each step.
Produce the exercise evidence described below.
explanation: Training computes predictions, measures a loss, differentiates it, and updates parameters. Inference uses fixed parameters to predict. Parameters are learned numbers; tokens are units of input; context length is how many positions the model can attend to. An activation is an intermediate value for one input, not a persistent parameter. Teacher forcing trains many next-token targets in parallel with a causal mask.

One forward pass can be used during both training and inference. Training additionally retains information needed for derivatives and updates the weights after measuring error. Autoregressive inference repeatedly feeds a growing prefix through the model; sampling a token does not by itself update any parameter.

lessons.title: A realistic Apple Silicon budget
lessons.why: The budget determines safe batch size, context, and architecture before an expensive run.
objectives: Explain a realistic apple silicon budget in your own words.
Work through the numerical example and justify each step.
Produce the exercise evidence described below.
explanation: CPU code is the simplest correctness reference. GPUs execute many similar operations in parallel and benefit from sufficiently large workloads. CUDA is NVIDIA’s platform; Metal is Apple’s compute API; MLX supplies arrays and autodiff optimized for Apple Silicon. Unified memory reduces some explicit transfers but does not make allocation free or capacity infinite. Measure your Mac rather than assuming a memory tier from its chip name.

Begin with a small benchmark that you can repeat in seconds. A larger parameter count changes not only the number of weights but also intermediate activations, matrix dimensions, optimizer storage, and how well the GPU is utilized. Therefore throughput from one tiny configuration cannot be extrapolated linearly without a measurement.

Use decimal MB for a rough parameter-storage calculation and binary GiB for operating-system memory capacity; label the units. Activity Monitor and runtime allocation counters measure different things. Leave room for the operating system, browser, compiler, and temporary training allocations. If memory pressure causes swapping, reduce the experiment before drawing performance conclusions.

lessons.title: Vectors, dot products & representations
lessons.why: An embedding is a learned vector; linear layers repeatedly compute weighted sums.
objectives: Explain vectors, dot products & representations in your own words.
Work through the numerical example and justify each step.
Produce the exercise evidence described below.
explanation: A scalar is one number. A vector is an ordered collection of numbers with a consistent interpretation for each coordinate. A tensor generalizes arrays to any number of axes. Addition combines corresponding coordinates; scaling multiplies them all. A dot product is a weighted sum and becomes a neuron’s basic computation. Its geometric interpretation is signed alignment, not a similarity bounded to [0,1].

An ordered list is meaningful only when you keep the coordinate convention fixed. If the first entry means height and the second means weight, swapping entries changes the input. Learned representations usually have no human-assigned meaning per coordinate, but their order must still be consistent across layers.

Implement the dot product with an accumulator initialized to zero. Verify symmetry and bilinearity on small examples: dot(a+b,c)=dot(a,c)+dot(b,c). These are useful properties, but they do not replace a concrete expected-value test because two incorrect implementations can agree with one another.

lessons.title: Matrices, transformations & shapes
lessons.why: GPT projections map a batch of token vectors into Q, K, V, and vocabulary logits.
objectives: Explain matrices, transformations & shapes in your own words.
Work through the numerical example and justify each step.

explanation: A matrix can represent a linear transformation or a batch of vectors. We use row-major storage and batch rows: X has B rows and D features, and W has D rows and H output features. Each output entry is a row-column dot product. A bias has H entries and is added to each batch row. Matrix multiplication is not elementwise multiplication.

A linear transformation is fully described by what it does to basis vectors. In the column-vector convention, matrix columns describe those images. In this course our batches contain row vectors, so we write XW; the same geometry is represented with the appropriate orientation. Consistency matters more than memorizing one convention.

lessons.title: Derivatives, partials & the chain rule
lessons.why: Backpropagation applies precisely this local rule across the full decoder graph.
objectives: Explain derivatives, partials & the chain rule in your own words.
Work through the numerical example and justify each step.
Produce the exercise evidence described below.
explanation: A derivative measures local sensitivity: how much the output changes per small input change. A partial derivative varies one coordinate while holding the others fixed. The gradient collects partial derivatives of a scalar loss. A Jacobian collects derivatives of a vector output. The chain rule multiplies sensitivities along a path and adds contributions from multiple paths.

For a scalar output with many inputs, the gradient tells you each input’s local influence while other inputs are held fixed. It is a local statement: a finite step can move into a region where the derivative changes. This is why an optimizer must recompute derivatives after every forward pass.

Centered differences use two function evaluations: [f(x+h)-f(x-h)]/(2h). Truncation error decreases with h for a smooth function, but floating-point cancellation eventually dominates. Sweep several h values and look for a stable agreement region instead of assuming the smallest h is best.

lessons.title: Probability, logarithms & cross-entropy
lessons.why: Every GPT output position contributes a next-token negative log likelihood.
objectives: Explain probability, logarithms & cross-entropy in your own words.
Work through the numerical example and justify each step.
Produce the exercise evidence described below.
explanation: A discrete distribution assigns nonnegative probabilities summing to one. Conditional probability uses available context. Expectation is a probability-weighted average. Entropy measures uncertainty; cross-entropy measures how much probability a model assigns to targets from another distribution. Natural logarithms make products of sequence probabilities into sums. A one-hot target gives loss -log p(correct).

Imagine paying a penalty whenever your model is surprised by the true outcome. Giving probability 1 to that outcome costs zero; giving probability 0.01 costs about 4.605 nats. The penalty becomes arbitrarily large as target probability approaches zero. This is why confident mistakes matter even if top-1 accuracy is unchanged.

The model distribution p is compared with a target distribution q. For next-token training q is usually one-hot, so the entire sum reduces to the target log probability. Entropy is the special case where the two distributions match. Conditional language modeling repeats this comparison for each context in the dataset.

lessons.title: Floating-point stability & gradient descent
lessons.why: Optimization and stability are prerequisites for every successful training run.
objectives: Explain floating-point stability & gradient descent in your own words.
Work through the numerical example and justify each step.
Produce the exercise evidence described below.
explanation: Floating-point arithmetic rounds, so algebraically identical formulas can behave differently. A gradient points uphill locally. Subtracting a small multiple of it moves downhill for a sufficiently small step. The learning rate controls this step; too large a rate can oscillate or diverge. Use stable formulas and double-precision references before optimizing.

For the quadratic, subtract the optimum from both sides of the update: w_next-3=(1-2η)(w-3). The distance shrinks exactly when |1-2η|<1, which gives 0<η<1. At η=1 the sign flips without shrinking; above 1 the magnitude grows. This derivation explains the observed trajectory rather than merely naming it divergence.

Stable formulas preserve the mathematical function while avoiding avoidable overflow or cancellation. Start with float64 to make debugging easier; later compare float32 against it. A finite result is necessary but not sufficient: always compare to an independent worked fixture.
